messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 26
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Bank Teller
  trauma_type: Terrorism
  pcl5: 43

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Overwork: work excessively to avoid being alone with thoughts, Avoid Intimacy: Being emotionally close or intimate with others, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Threat: Irritability: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively, Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe, Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
  Negative Appraisals: No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Anh's Vigilance

Anh Tran was twenty-three when the bomb went off at the transit station three blocks from his apartment in Portland. He had been on his way home from his shift at the bank, earbuds in, thinking about the dinner his wife Linh had texted him about—something with lemongrass and pork. The blast came without warning. A sound so loud it erased all other sounds, followed by a pressure that lifted him off his feet and threw him against a concrete pillar. When his hearing returned in fragments, he heard screaming, saw people with blood on their faces, and felt a terrible clarity that he was alive and many others were not. He had lain on the ground for what felt like hours, waiting for the second explosion that emergency responders later said never came—but in those minutes, Anh was certain it would.

Three years have passed, and Anh is now twenty-six, divorced, and sitting in the break room of the First National Bank on Morrison Street with his third energy drink of the day. He has been at work since 5:45 a.m., before the branch opened, and he will stay until at least 7 p.m., long after his shift ends. His supervisor has stopped asking why. The work itself—the precise movements of counting cash, the repetitive nature of processing transactions, the structured interaction with customers—keeps his mind occupied in a way that sleep never does. At night, when there is nothing to do but exist in the quiet of his apartment, his thoughts turn inward, and he has learned that this is unbearable. So he volunteers for extra hours, takes on tasks no one else wants, and fills every moment with something that demands his attention. His colleagues assume he is ambitious. Only Anh knows he is running.

The marriage to Linh had ended a year after the bombing. She had wanted him to talk about what happened, to let her in, to be the person she had married. But Anh could not do this. The thought of sitting across from her, of being vulnerable, of allowing someone to see the full extent of his fear and shame, felt like a kind of exposure he could not survive. He had begun sleeping in the spare room. When she tried to touch him, he flinched. When she asked him questions about his day, his jaw would clench and he would snap at her—not because she had done anything wrong, but because the act of being asked, of being required to engage emotionally, made him furious. Eventually, she stopped trying. The divorce papers were signed quietly. He has not been in a relationship since, and the thought of it now—of another person knowing him, expecting things from him, being disappointed by him—fills him with a dread he cannot quite name.

What frightens Anh most is the conviction that he is no longer the person he was before the bomb. He had been competent, reliable, someone Linh could depend on. Now he cannot depend on himself. He cannot trust his own mind. His thoughts betray him—they return to the bombing unbidden, and when they do, he pushes them away with such force that he sometimes feels something crack inside his chest. He has come to believe that if he allows himself to think about what happened, even for a moment, he will be consumed by it. So he does not think about it. He works. He stays busy. He checks behind himself when he walks, a habit so ingrained now that he does it without noticing—in the bank, on the street, in the grocery store. His eyes scan for exits, for crowds, for anything that might conceal a threat. At night, he wakes in a state of high alert, sometimes two or three times, to verify that his apartment is secure, that no one has breached the locks, that he is safe. Most mornings, he is exhausted before the day has begun.

Last week, a customer came through his line carrying a large backpack. Anh's hands began to shake. He excused himself and spent twenty minutes in the bathroom, breathing into the sink. When he returned, the customer was gone, but so was something in Anh—some final thread of the person he thought he could still be. He called a therapist that evening. He does not yet know what help might look like, or whether he is capable of receiving it, but he knows that he cannot continue as he is. The work, the checking, the sleepless nights, the wall he has built between himself and the world—none of it has made him safe. All it has done is made him profoundly, irrevocably alone.
